dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematic front-loaded read of every major reference file (app.rb, all models, middleware/helpers, jobs, migrations, seeds, templates, specs), plus dumping the reference DB schema (64) and reading rack-protection gem internals (53-58) to recover exact CSP/protection defaults instead of guessing.

Empirical orientation: booted the reference, generated a golden corpus, then ran the live reference on :8001 with a purpose-built dual-differ using shared IDs — confirming behavior against the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
Probed edge-case contracts empirically: halt/404/401/403/410 bodies, header sets, HttpOrigin 403 protection and its headers, vary/304 conditional-GET, admin audit/queue edges.

Reverse-engineered the hard-to-guess subsystems: cross-runtime shared job queue, dead-letter behavior via injected failures, and shared-DB schema compatibility — the exact BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry semantics the task flags as parity risks.

Sustained re-probing mid-build: when tag rendering/validation mismatches surfaced, agent went back to the reference to inspect tag joins, post-with-tags responses, and validation behavior rather than assuming.
Wrote durable memory notes capturing the recovered behavioral model, indicating orientation was recorded, not just transient.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent methodically mapped each subsystem to reference behavior from BOTH exhaustive source reading (including gem internals and schema dumps) AND live probing of the running reference via a dual-differ, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, validation errors, CSP, HttpOrigin, dead-letter, claim semantics) empirically — matching the level-8 anchor. It also sustained orientation across the entire horizon, repeatedly revisiting the reference to resolve new mismatches (tags, blockquotes, HttpOrigin, admin edges) and recording a durable model, pushing toward level 10; I hold at 9 only because the condensed log doesn't let me confirm the notes were an exhaustive contract table.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Explicit ordered TaskCreate milestone breakdown: skeleton/health+deps → DB schema+seed → headers/rate-limit/audit/etag → CRUD/sessions/search/media/admin → markdown → templates/routes → job runner. Dependency-aware sequencing (schema & header contracts before feeds/CRUD), written down as discrete tasks.
TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress/completed) across the run show the milestone plan is actively referenced and tracked to completion, not abandoned.
Per-subsystem differential parity harnesses (compare.py, diff.py, diff2/3.py, fuzz.py) give each milestone a concrete exit/done-check.
Cross-runtime shared job-queue and dead-letter parity validated late rather than de-risked first; the hardest shared-state coupling was not front-loaded, keeping this below the 10 anchor.

Reconnaissance phase precedes and informs the milestone plan, but the plan set at 67-73 stays largely static (marked complete rather than reshaped), so it does not reach the 'revised as complexity reshapes plan' bar of 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, written, dependency-aware milestone plan (TaskCreate steps 67-73) with sensible ordering — foundational schema and header contracts early — and each subsystem carried a concrete differential parity check, matching the 8 anchor; the plan was referenced and tracked via TaskUpdate throughout. It stops short of 10 because the hardest cross-runtime interface (shared job-queue claim/dead-letter semantics) was verified late rather than sequenced first to de-risk, and the milestone set was largely static rather than revised as complexity emerged.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Generated a golden corpus from the reference early, establishing an oracle baseline for later differential comparison.

Built reusable diff harnesses (compare.py, diff.py), booted the REAL reference server on :8001, ran the same requests against both with shared IDs, and iterated on encoding — a genuine differential oracle mirroring the grader's side-by-side approach.

Extended coverage to byte-exact media upload parity, cross-runtime shared job queue, concurrency smoke test, latency parity benchmark, and diff3.py extended differential — spanning most subsystems and the shared-queue interop.
Checked hard constraints (binary size, no-Ruby compliance), ran randomized fuzz comparison across seeds, dead-letter parity with injected failures, and cross-runtime schema compatibility.
Repeatedly re-ran golden/diff comparisons as regression sweeps after fixes, using the harness as a recurring gate through the end of the run.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 8: it built multiple reusable differential harnesses that run identical requests against the real reference server, elide/normalize dynamic values, cover nearly all subsystems, and exercise the cross-runtime job queue (including dead-letter). It also reaches into anchor 10 with concurrency tests, shared-queue claim/interop, latency-ratio and byte-exact media checks, hard-constraint (no-Ruby/binary-size) verification, and repeated regression sweeps. I place it at 9 rather than 10 because the index-only evidence does not let me confirm the normalization faithfully reproduces every grader rule and the harness was manually re-run rather than a fully automated continuous gate.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Created a structured subsystem task list (TaskCreate) covering skeleton/DB/headers/CRUD/markdown/routes/jobs — establishes a done-vs-remaining ledger across subsystems.
TaskUpdate statuses (in_progress→completed) are updated as pieces pass, showing the coverage ledger is actively maintained across the horizon, not just at the start.
Built and repeatedly re-ran differential harnesses (compare.py/diff.py/diff2/diff3), giving harness-backed pass/fail signal per subsystem.
Explicit regression checks and a final regression sweep after fixes touching shared code — guards against regressing previously-passing areas.
Investigated a specific fuzz seed 7 failure and confirmed search converges after job processing rather than looping, i.e. recognized a stuck point and diagnosed it.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a subsystem task ledger it updates as pieces pass (steps 67-73, 97, 255-258) and backs it with differential harnesses re-run after changes, plus explicit regression sweeps (306, 321, 354) that guard against regressing passing areas — matching the level-8 anchor. It also diagnoses a specific failing case instead of looping (356-358). It falls short of level 10 because the ledger is coarse and there is no precise, continuously-maintained passing/failing/not-yet-attempted accounting used to prioritize the highest-value gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Built compare.py differ, ran trace comparison; identified a CLASS of failures ('bare halt bodies'/'bare status responses'), probed how Sinatra renders halt bodies (173-179), then systematically replaced all bare status responses and rebuilt+recompared — recognizing a failure class rather than one-off patching.

Stood up live dual differ against the reference, ran verbose JSON/HTML diffs, and on tag-rendering mismatch went back to inspect reference tag joins (212-214) before removing the tag separator space — return-to-reference correction.

Markdown/Rouge subsystem re-derived across repeated rounds: probed blockquote merging, unknown-lang fallback, mapped Rouge lexer tags; each fix followed by rebuild+golden retest — treating recurring mismatches in one subsystem as signal and re-verifying the whole subsystem.

A diff surfaced missing HttpOrigin protection; agent read the protection source, tested it on the reference, checked 403 headers, edited server.rs, verified parity, then ran a regression check — root-caused, corrected, confirmed no regression.

Tag/status/visibility validation edge cases re-derived from reference behavior (271-296) with multiple route edits and re-tests for 500/validation parity — iterative correction grounded in reference probing.

Investigated fuzz seed-7 failure, confirmed search converges after job processing, and tested dead-letter parity with injected failures — chasing residual divergences to root cause late in the horizon.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never papers over mismatches; every diff triggers a return to the reference to recover true behavior, correct, and re-verify (above anchor 3/5). It goes further than local fixes on several occasions — systematically eliminating a bare-status-response failure class and re-deriving the markdown/Rouge subsystem across multiple rounds with full golden retests plus regression sweeps (anchor 8 territory). However, corrections stay mostly targeted rather than sweeping design overhauls, and there is no decisive library/model swap forced by an unreachable-parity constraint (anchor 10), so it lands at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Chose tiny_http/rusqlite/serde_json/bcrypt/sha2 — deliberately non-Ruby-bridge crate selection, satisfying the Cargo.toml prohibition by design.
Job runner built with BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, dead-letter from the start — shared-DB claim semantics treated as a matched contract, not an afterthought.

Repeated cross-runtime tests of the shared job queue, injected-failure dead-letter parity, and shared-DB schema compatibility against the live reference — the hardest interop constraint verified multiple times.
Explicit latency parity benchmark — monitors the p99/p50 latency-ratio constraint.
'Binary size and compliance checks' — verifies the 40 MB cap and Ruby-runtime prohibitions, but appears as a single check in the verification phase rather than a continuously re-run gate.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guarded each hard constraint during development: chose non-Ruby crates by design (67), monitored binary size/compliance (323), benchmarked latency parity (259), and treated the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter as a matched contract re-verified against the live reference (73, 251, 360, 379) — squarely the anchor-8 profile. It falls short of 10 because the size/latency/no-Ruby checks read as one-time verifications in the late phase rather than standing regression gates that would catch a violation the moment it was introduced.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
